title: An Experience Report on a Pedagogically Controlled, Curriculum-Constrained AI Tutor for SE Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how a large-language-model-based tutor can be integrated into secondary computer science / software engineering education in a way that is pedagogically controlled and constrained to curriculum content. The authors argue that generic AI chatbots are often too open-ended for educational use, so they explore an approach that preserves instructional safety, reduces hallucinations, and supports learners without replacing teachers.

The intervention is RockStartIT Tutor, an AI assistant powered by GPT-4/GPT-4o via OpenAI’s Assistant API. Rather than fine-tuning a model, the system uses a modular, tagged Markdown knowledge base and prompt engineering to keep responses grounded in approved course material, deliver hints before solutions, and maintain age-appropriate language. The tutor also uses threaded conversation memory and streaming responses to support multi-turn interaction in a web-based interface.

The evaluation involved 13 participants: 7 learners and 6 teachers/prospective teachers, all working with the tutor during a RockStartIT course on programming and computational thinking. Participants completed a TAM-based questionnaire and answered open-ended questions after a 30–45 minute use session on their own devices. Results suggested generally positive perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use, with teachers especially valuing the tutor as a complement to instruction and learners appreciating the low-pressure environment for asking questions.

The main conclusion is that a carefully constrained AI tutor can be acceptable and potentially useful in secondary-level computing education when it is tightly aligned to curriculum content and used as a support tool rather than a replacement for teachers. The study also highlights several design challenges, including onboarding, trust calibration, and the need for longer-term studies with the intended age group.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample mixed-methods pilot/experience report (n=13) using self-report TAM measures and qualitative feedback, not a controlled efficacy study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about acceptability and use, but limited credibility for causal claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive acceptance and perceived support value, but it does not report learning gains or robust outcome effects. Impact is therefore unclear/modest rather than demonstrably strong.

interventions.use_case: pedagogically controlled GPT-4o chat tutor for a secondary school programming and computational thinking course, using curriculum-constrained responses, hint-first scaffolding, and threaded dialogue

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally reported that the AI tutor created a low-stakes, nonjudgmental environment that made it easier to ask questions and receive support. The study used a TAM-style questionnaire with n=13 and found strong perceived usefulness and ease of use ratings, especially on items related to clarity and comfort with interaction (e.g., PEOU1 M=4.54, PEOU2 M=4.62).
finding.measure: Technology Acceptance Model questionnaire items and open-ended feedback on usability, helpfulness, and future use

finding.finding_summary: The tutor was reported to support inquiry, reflection, and metacognitive thinking by giving hints rather than direct solutions. Qualitative comments indicated that it helped users trace reasoning errors and understand concepts, aligning with the paper’s emphasis on scaffolded problem solving and critical thinking; however, no formal learning gain effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended responses and TAM items related to usefulness for understanding tasks and learning support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the tutor as a useful classroom support tool that could reduce cognitive load and complement instruction, with strong agreement that it could be a useful addition to teaching materials (PU8 M=4.5, SD=0.54). The study did not measure actual workload reduction, but teacher acceptance and comments suggest perceived efficiency benefits rather than demonstrated performance gains.
finding.measure: Teacher TAM items on usefulness, classroom support, and intention to use
